entities.evidence: Yahweh is the personal name of the speaker, whom the text calls Yahweh God. He promises to make a helper for the man and brings the woman to him in Gen.2.22.

analysis.evidence: יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים is the subject of וַיֹּאמֶר. The direct speech opens with לֹא טוֹב (“it is not good”) and continues with the speaker’s first-person אֶעֱשֶׂהּ (“I will make”).
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־

analysis.evidence: In וַיֹּאמֶר יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים (“Yahweh God said”), יַהְוֶה names the speaker, and אֱלֹהִים stands in apposition.
analysis.morphology: Proper noun, masculine singular, without prefix or suffix
analysis.sense: Personal name of the God of Israel

analysis.evidence: In וַיֹּאמֶר יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהִים, אֱלֹהִים stands in apposition to יַהְוֶה. The singular verb וַיֹּאמֶר (‘he said’) and the speaker’s אֶעֱשֶׂהּ (‘I will make’) identify one speaker.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine plural absolute, with a singular referent.

analysis.evidence: לֹא negates the predicate adjective טוֹב. God states that it is not good for the man to be alone.
analysis.morphology: Negative particle without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: לֹא negates טוֹב, and הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ names the situation being judged: “It is not good for the man to be alone.” God’s decision to make a helper for him shows that the judgment concerns the suitability of his solitary state.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular absolute adjective, used predicatively.
analysis.sense: good in quality, fine, fit for use

analysis.evidence: In הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ, הָאָדָם is the subject of the infinitive and לְבַדּוֹ describes his condition. לֹא טוֹב evaluates that whole situation: “It is not good for the man to be alone.”
analysis.morphology: Qal infinitive construct, without prefix or suffix
analysis.sense: to be in a state or condition

analysis.evidence: In הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ, “for the man to be alone,” the article identifies the particular man under discussion. The masculine singular suffixes in לְבַדּוֹ (“by himself”) and לּוֹ (“for him”) refer back to him.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הָ־ prefixed to a masculine singular absolute common noun.

analysis.evidence: In הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ, the suffix refers to the man and the phrase describes him as being by himself. God’s promise to make him עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ, a helper corresponding to him, confirms this sense.
analysis.morphology: Preposition לְ + masculine singular construct noun בַּד + third-person masculine singular suffix וֹ, referring to הָאָדָם. The whole expression functions adverbially.

analysis.evidence: God has said that it is not good for the man to be alone. עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ supplies the object, “a helper corresponding to him,” and לּוֹ identifies the beneficiary, “for him.”
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, first person common singular, expressing intention. The packet marks the final ה with a mappiq, but the syntax supports reading the verb without a pronominal suffix.

draft.evidence: In Gen.2.18 the suffix on לּוֹ refers back to הָאָדָם. God will make a helper for him.

Leviticus 23 sets the appointed times down with לְ two ways: each is "to Yahweh" (a sabbath לַיהוָה, Lev 23:3; a passover לַיהוָה, Lev 23:5), and each is "to you", a holy convocation and a sabbath of rest לָכֶם (Lev 23:7, 32). They are Yahweh's own ("these are my appointed times", Lev 23:2), and given for his people's good: "Yahweh has given you the sabbath" (Exo 16:29). Jesus says the same of the sabbath: "the sabbath was made for man, not man for the sabbath" (Mrk 2:27).

Root investigation (2026-11-13). No root is viable; the entry is keyed by its own consonant ל, as min is keyed מנ. (1) The particle is one consonant with a short vowel in every language that has it (Hebrew lə-, Aramaic and Syriac l-, Ugaritic l /li-/, Phoenician l-, Sabaic l-, Ge'ez la-, Arabic li-/la-), and with suffixes it is built on that letter alone (לוֹ, לָכֶם; Ugaritic lh, lkm; Arabic lahu, lakum), with no third-weak base such as עַל (עָלָיו, from עלה) and אֶל (אֵלָיו) show. So nothing in its form points to a longer root. (2) The verb לָוָה "join, attach" (Gen 29:34; Num 18:2, 4; Isa 56:3, 6) has a sense near "belonging to", but no cognate dictionary derives l- from lwy and the suffixed forms show no w or y: rejected. (3) אֶל: kept apart. Hebrew, Phoenician and Arabic each have both words side by side with different ranges (Phoenician l- "never of direction", Krahmalkov p. 248; Arabic li- and ʾilā); אֶל has a longer y-base and לְ none; and Ugaritic has l but no ʾl "to". אֶל is a word of the elah entry (root אלה), not of el-al (which holds the negative אַל, root אלל); nothing here proposes moving it. (4) Akkadian has no l- preposition (ana, ina); Segert's "Akkad. < Aram. la" is a late loan from Aramaic and is not cited. Amorite la (Segert p. 190) is noted only. Not checked: Dillmann for Ge'ez ለ (only Wiktionary cited); Payne Smith for Syriac ܠ (SEDRA only); CAL for Aramaic. Left out: the conditional לוּ (l.ar.aa, in lo.json), the emphatic or vocative la- some see in Hebrew, and the compounds BDB files elsewhere: לִפְנֵי (panah), לְמַעַן (under ענה), לָכֵן (l.bp.ag, "see כֵּן"), לָמָּה (מָה). The Hebrew letter's own BDB key l.aa.aa ("twelfth letter") is not claimed. Token counts: the corpus links no token to l.aa.ab. OSHB tags every suffixed form (לִי, לוֹ, לָכֶם, לָהֶם …, about 4,500 tokens, and about 60 in the Aramaic) with the bare lemma "l" and no Strong's number, and the generator's build_surface_entries only links lemmas with a number, so lexicon-support will show no uses for לְ or its Aramaic until that is fixed. The prefixed לְ is a proclitic counted under the word it joins, as with מִן. The senses are illustrated, not exhaustive.

analysis.evidence: הָאָדָם is the man described as alone. In אֶעֱשֶׂהּ לּוֹ עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ, עֵזֶר names what God will make, and לּוֹ identifies the man for whom he will make the helper.
analysis.morphology: Preposition לְ with the third-person masculine singular pronominal suffix ־וֹ.

analysis.evidence: The man is לְבַדּוֹ (“alone”). God says he will make לּוֹ (“for him”) an עֵזֶר, and כְּנֶגְדּוֹ describes that helper as someone corresponding to him.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine singular absolute, without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: a helper, one who is help

analysis.evidence: In עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ, the suffix refers to הָאָדָם. His being alone (לְבַדּוֹ) prompts the promise of a helper who corresponds to him as his counterpart.
analysis.morphology: Preposition כְּ־ (as, like) + preposition נֶגֶד (opposite, facing) + third-person masculine singular pronominal suffix ־וֹ (him).
analysis.sense: (כְּנֶגְדּוֹ) as in front of him: corresponding to him, his counterpart
